food.text: The Neolithic Revolution reached Europe beginning in 7000–6500 BC. Agriculturalists from the Near East entered the Greek peninsula from Anatolia by island-hopping through the Aegean Sea, bringing farming with them.
The earliest known Neolithic sites in Europe with developed agricultural economies were found in Greece. They are dated to 8500–9000 BP, which makes Greece a pioneer of European farming.

Neolithic Greece began with the establishment of agricultural societies around 7,000 BC and lasted until about 3,200 BC. It was the base for the early Bronze Age civilizations in the area, and the first organized communities developed during it.

In Neolithic Greece, the northern Thessalian plain had enough rainfall for dry-farming, which allowed densely populated settlements. In southern Greece, such as the Peloponesus, early villages were more dispersed and sprang up around small arable tracts close to springs, lakes, and marshes.

Bitter vetch was present in Greece from at least 8000 BCE. Most ancient literature that mentions it describes it as animal food with a disagreeable taste. It was considered a famine food, and it was only occasionally eaten in Classical times.
Millet was growing wild in Greece as early as 3000 BCE. Centuries later Hesiod wrote that the beards grow round the millet, which men sow in summer.

Thessalian tells, the mounds built up from the debris of successive settlements, often reflect small hamlets with a population of around 40–80. They stood in the northern plain where rainfall was sufficient for dry-farming.

art.text: The oldest golden artifacts in the world, dated to 4600 BC to 4200 BC, come from the Varna Necropolis in Bulgaria. They were grave offerings, and they are now displayed in the Varna Archaeological Museum.

Neolithic Greece, which began when farming arrived in 7000 to 6500 BC, saw architectural innovations such as "megaron-type" and "Tsangli-type" houses. It was also a time of elaborate art and tool manufacturing.

Neolithic Greece was an important base for the early Bronze Age civilizations of the area. It was in this period that the first organized communities developed and basic art became more advanced, before the era ended around 3200 BC.

In parts of the Balkans, the period after about 5000 BC is called the Chalcolithic, or Copper Age. The name comes from the invention of copper smelting and the spread of copper tools, weapons and other objects. Copper was in use across the Balkans from about 3500 BC.

In the Early Neolithic period, Greek communities developed pottery technology that involved the successful firing of vases. At this time settlements still consisted of independent one-room huts, each community home to 50 to 100 people.

The Mycenaean megaron grew out of the megaroid, a large hall-centered rectangular building of mainland Greece dating back to the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age. It later became the architectural precursor to the Greek temples of the Archaic and Classical periods.

Solnitsata supplied salt throughout the Balkans, and a large collection of gold objects nearby has led archaeologists to think this trade made its residents wealthy. The gold is linked to the Varna Necropolis.

In parts of Europe, notably the Balkans, the period after c. 5000 BC is known as the Chalcolithic, or Copper Age. The name reflects the invention of copper smelting and the prevalence of copper tools, weapons and other artifacts.

Obsidian from the volcanic island of Milos was used to make tools and weapons, and it travelled across the Aegean and mainland Greece. Its oldest finding off the island, dated 9000 to 7800 BC, was at the Franchthi cave in the Argolid.

Solnitsata's inner and outer city included a pottery production site alongside its salt facility. Although its population is estimated at only 350, Vassil Nikolov argues it meets the criteria for a prehistoric proto-city.

In the Final Neolithic, or Chalcolithic, Greece's farming population began to import bronze and copper. They used basic bronze-working techniques first developed in Asia Minor, with which they had cultural contacts.

war.text: The Neolithic walls of Sesklo and Dimini in Thessaly were first called defensive and military by their excavator, Christos Tsountas, who dug there between 1899 and 1906. The remains at Sesklo show extensive burning and destruction, which the article calls significant evidence for conflict, and there is information suggesting Dimini may be to blame. The article also cautions that the burning could have had other causes, such as flammable building materials, and that many archaeologists now see the walls as retaining walls, animal enclosures, markers of living space or ritual structures.

An "invasion theory" holds that the Sesklo culture lasted more than a thousand years, until about 5000 BC. It says the people of the Dimini culture then violently conquered it. Sesklo had been a large settlement, covering about 20 hectares at its peak.

The Neolithic walls of Sesklo and Dimini in Thessaly were first claimed by their excavator Christos Tsountas to be defensive. Over time many archaeologists have argued instead that they were retaining walls, animal enclosures, markers of habitation space, or ritual features. Either way, the walls reinforced the distinction between the inner settlement and the outside world.

The volcanic island of Milos was visited for its obsidian, which was used to make tools and weapons, from the Mesolithic until the late Neolithic. Its oldest finds off the island, dated 9000 to 7800 BC, come from Franchthi Cave in the Argolid. Milos stone travelled across the Aegean and mainland Greece.

The walls of Sesklo and Dimini had baffle gates, which forced attackers to turn left and expose their unshielded right side. Sesklo had one on its western side, the side not protected by a steep ravine. Dimini had four or five, plus narrow openings that were easy to defend and would slow and confuse invaders.

At Varna in Bulgaria, Grave 43 held the oldest known burial of an elite man, dated to about 4495 BC. He was buried with remarkable amounts of gold, held a war axe or mace, and wore a gold penis sheath or possibly a decorative gold belt tip. Some authors have called the Varna elite males 'kings'.

The large Vinča settlements of the Balkans have been described as lacking any specialised military, religious or administrative centres, yet their settlements did have defensive formations. Vinča sites like Divostin and Crkvine-Stubline may have held thousands of people, with Divostin estimated at 868 to 2,864 and Crkvine-Stubline at up to 4,000. Marija Gimbutas pictured the Vinča culture as part of a peaceful Old Europe, but from the 1990s evidence began to emerge of violent massacres and defensively-enclosed fortified settlements in the Neolithic period.

Evidence for conflict in Neolithic Thessaly includes large empty areas of land that may have worked as buffer zones between settlements at war, exposing invaders as they crossed toward an opposing settlement. The remains at Sesklo show extensive burning and destruction, and there is information suggesting Dimini may be to blame, though the burning could have had other causes such as flammable building materials. The walls at both settlements had baffle gates, which forced invaders to turn left and expose their unshielded right side. Dimini had 4 or 5 such gates, while Sesklo had one on its western side.

An "invasion theory" states that the people of the Neolithic Dimini culture were responsible for the violent conquest of the Sesklo culture at around 5000 BC, and treats the "Diminians" and the "Seskloans" as two separate cultural entities. Ioannis Lyritzis and R. Galloway compared ceramics from both sites using thermoluminescence dating and found that the Dimini settlement appeared around 4800 BC, four centuries before the fall of the Sesklo civilization (ca. 4400 BC). Lyritzis concluded that the two peoples coexisted for a period of time.

Weapons found at Sesklo include stone projectile points, clay and stone sling bullets, axes and knives. If these weapons were used in a warfare context, fortified sites would have provided necessary defense and protection. The article notes that many of them could have had other purposes, including hunting.

Large empty areas of land act as buffer zones to separate settlements at war and expose invaders as they cross them to approach an opposing settlement, giving defenders the opportunity to prepare. The presence of such no man's lands in Thessaly indicates there may have been conflict and a need for defensive fortifications. Makriyalos in Pieria and Strofilas on Andros Island have fortifications whose military function has been argued very convincingly.

Dimini largely controlled the production and exchange of an exotic, valuable oyster shell used for rings, beads and buttons. It was limited to a few elites as a sign of status. Fortifications would have protected this valuable asset, and the walls also suggest a lack of trust between neighbouring settlements.

Among the gold in the Varna cemetery were bull-shaped gold platelets. They perhaps venerated virility, instinctive force and warfare, and a proto-castle cult. They lay in a cemetery where the richest male burial held a war axe or mace and a gold penis sheath, or possibly a decorative gold belt tip.

science.text: Solnitsata, near the modern city of Provadia in Bulgaria, is the oldest salt production center in continental Europe, active from 5500 to 4200 BC. It was a fortified stone settlement with a salt production facility, and it flourished around 4700 to 4200 BC. Some call it the first prehistoric urban center in Europe.
The Vinča culture featured the earliest known example of copper smelting. It occupied a region of Southeast Europe corresponding mainly to modern Serbia and Kosovo, and was dated to 5400 to 4500 BC.

In the Balkans, the period after about 5000 BC is known as the Chalcolithic, or Copper Age, because of the invention of copper smelting. Copper tools, weapons and other artifacts became common. From 3500 BC copper was in use in the Balkans and across eastern and central Europe.

Some residential buildings at Solnitsata are thought to have been two stories tall, which suggests relatively advanced architectural planning for the prehistoric period. The settlement was walled to protect its salt, a crucial commodity in antiquity. The town is believed to have been destroyed by an earthquake.

A 2016 archaeogenetic study of samples from Greece and northwestern Anatolia showed that farming spread into Europe through demic diffusion, meaning migrating farmers, rather than through hunter-gatherers adopting it. Early Aegean farmers were directly linked genetically to Neolithic farmers across Europe, and all originated from farming communities of western Anatolia.

Vinča-Belo Brdo was discovered by the Serbian archaeologist Miloje Vasić in 1908 as a large tell settlement. Radiocarbon dating refined its span over time, from 76 dates in 1996 to 155 dates in 2009 and 600 dates in 2016. The latest work concluded the culture existed between 5400/5300 and 4500 BC.

There is no evidence of settlements on Milos until the Final Neolithic, around 4000 BC. Obsidian seems to have been gathered by groups of different people landing intermittently on the island to collect stone for making tools.

Solnitsata is believed to have supplied salt throughout the Balkans. A large collection of gold objects nearby, at the Varna Necropolis, has led archaeologists to think this trade brought great wealth to the town's residents. Vassil Nikolov argues the town meets the criteria for a prehistoric proto-city, though its population is estimated at only 350.

Obsidian from the island of Milos was transported across the Aegean, mainland Greece and Western Anatolia, and possibly as far as Egypt. Its oldest finds off the island come from Franchthi Cave in the Argolid, dated 9000 to 7800 BC. Groups of different people seem to have landed intermittently on Milos to collect stone for tools.

politics.text: Around 6300 to 6000 BCE, the Mesolithic site of Lepenski Vir on the Danube has been described as "the first city in Europe". This is despite its people living by foraging. The label comes from its permanence, organisation, and the sophistication of its architecture and construction.

The Varna Necropolis in Bulgaria offers the oldest known burial evidence of an elite man. The high status man buried with the most remarkable amount of gold held a war adze or mace and wore a gold penis sheath, or likely a belt tip made of gold. Bull-shaped gold platelets might also have venerated virility, instinctual force, and warfare. The culture had sophisticated religious beliefs about the afterlife and had developed hierarchical status differences.

Vinča culture settlements were some of the largest in prehistoric Europe. They kept a high degree of cultural uniformity through long-distance exchange of ritual items, but were probably not politically unified. One assessment finds no evidence for proto-urbanism or for specialised military, religious or administrative centres, yet the settlements did have defensive formations.

The Carnac tumuli were contemporary with the rich burials of the Varna culture in Bulgaria, around 4500 BC. The Varna burials show that powerful elites existed in southeastern Europe at the same time as they appeared in Carnac. Grave 43 at Varna held a man buried with a sceptre, gold ornaments and an Alpine jade axehead.

Lepenski Vir consisted of one large settlement with around ten satellite villages. Its seven successive settlements included the remains of 136 residential and sacral buildings, dating from 9500/7200 BC to 6000 BC. Archaeologist Dragoslav Srejović, who first explored the site, saw it as a very early and specific phase in European development.

Three graves at Varna held gold objects that together made up more than half of the total weight of all gold grave goods in the cemetery. A scepter, a symbol of supreme secular or religious authority, was found in each of these three graves. Some authors have described the Varna elite males as 'kings'. The elite male of Grave 43 was buried with remarkable amounts of gold, held a war axe or mace, and wore a gold penis sheath or possibly a decorative gold belt tip.

culture.text: Genetic studies show that farming reached Europe in the 7th millennium BC through a mass migration of people from Northwest Anatolia to Southeast Europe. Almost all (c. 98%) of the local Balkan hunter-gatherer gene pool was replaced with ancestry from Anatolian farmers. Farming was carried by people, not just by ideas, and the article says the relationship between farmers and hunter-gatherers was not always peaceful.

Sesklo was a significant Neolithic settlement in Thessaly. At its peak around 5000 BC it covered about 20 hectares and had roughly 500 to 800 houses. Its population may have been as large as 5,000 people.

Sesklo culture produced an abundance of statuettes of women, often pregnant. They are probably connected to widely hypothesized prehistoric fertility cults. Similar figures appear in all the Balkan cultures and most of the Danube civilization across many millennia.

The Vinča culture, dated to 5400 to 4500 BC, was noted for its distinctive dark-burnished pottery. Its settlements were among the largest in prehistoric Europe. They kept a high degree of cultural uniformity through the long-distance exchange of ritual items, though they were probably not politically unified.

The Varna Necropolis in Bulgaria holds the oldest golden artifacts in the world, dated between 4600 BC and 4200 BC. They were found as grave offerings and are now displayed in the Varna Archaeological Museum.

Vinča culture is known for zoomorphic and anthropomorphic figurines and for the Vinča symbols. Some conjecture that these symbols are the earliest form of proto-writing. The culture also featured the earliest known example of copper smelting.

The Starčevo culture, dating between about 6200 and 4500 BCE, brought farming and ceramics into the inland Balkans. It grew out of the spread of Neolithic peoples from Asia Minor. Its type site lies on the north bank of the Danube near Starčevo in Serbia, opposite Belgrade.

At its peak around 5000 BC, the Neolithic settlement of Sesklo covered about 20 hectares and comprised about 500 to 800 houses, with a population estimated to be potentially as large as 5,000 people. According to an "invasion theory", the Sesklo culture lasted more than a millennium, until c. 5000 BC, when it was violently conquered by people of the Dimini culture. Professor Ioannis Lyritzis argues against this: thermoluminescence dating suggests the Dimini people first appeared among the "Seskloans" c. 4800 BC, and that the two groups co-existed for a time.

Vinča settlements were considerably larger than almost all other contemporary European cultures. In some cases their size surpassed the cities of the Aegean and early Near Eastern Bronze Age a millennium later. One of the largest sites, Vinča-Belo Brdo, covered 29 hectares with up to 2,500 people.

The type site of the Vinča culture, Vinča-Belo Brdo, is a large tell settlement discovered by Serbian archaeologist Miloje Vasić in 1908. Radiocarbon dating has been refined over time. In 2016, 600 dates concluded that the culture existed between 5400/5300 and 4500 BC.
Marija Gimbutas mentions recognition of a gorgon mask from the Sesklo culture, dating from about 6000 BC. She notes it is an image that persisted throughout Ancient and Classical Greek arts.

Milos was visited for its obsidian, used to make tools and weapons, from the Mesolithic until the late Neolithic. Its stone travelled across the Aegean and mainland Greece. The oldest finds outside the island, at Franchthi cave, date to the Mesolithic (9000 to 7800 BC), and groups seem to have landed intermittently to resupply.

Vinča culture is known for the Vinča symbols, which some conjecture to be the earliest form of proto-writing. It was also noted for distinctive dark-burnished pottery and for zoomorphic and anthropomorphic figurines.

The Divostin site of the Vinča culture was occupied twice between 4900 and 4650 BC. An estimate based on 17 houses and a house lifespan of 56 years suggests 1028 houses were built there. Its final population is estimated at between 868 and 2864 people.

Dating in 2020 showed that the two oldest Starčevo sites are Crkvina near Miokovci, Serbia and Runik, Kosovo, at about 6238 BCE and 6185 BCE. The site of Mavropigi is considered a more probable origin of the population movement than Sesklo. The people likely travelled along river routes.
